lead: Sinusoidal PWM (SPWM) compares a sine reference with a fast triangular carrier and switches the bridge at every crossing. The duty ratio then varies sinusoidally over the output cycle, so the average output follows the reference. The fundamental is set by the reference amplitude and its frequency by the reference frequency, while the unwanted harmonics move up to the carrier frequency, where a small filter or the load inductance removes them. Bipolar SPWM gives a two-level output; unipolar SPWM gives a three-level output with half the ripple.
prereq: You need: the full bridge and the idea of a variable pulse width from single and multiple pulse modulation.

blocks.text: Let the reference be v<sub>r</sub> = V<sub>r</sub> sin 2πf<sub>m</sub> t, with peak V<sub>r</sub> and frequency f<sub>m</sub> (the output frequency), and let the triangular carrier have peak V<sub>c</sub> and frequency f<sub>c</sub>. Each crossing of the two is a switching instant. Two ratios describe the modulator.
ma = Vr/Vc, mf = fc/fm ma is the amplitude modulation index and mf the frequency modulation ratio.

In one carrier period the leg is on top for a fraction d = ½(1 + m<sub>a</sub> sin θ) of the time, so the average leg voltage, measured from the bus midpoint, is (V<sub>dc</sub>/2) m<sub>a</sub> sin θ. Its fundamental is a sine of peak m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub>/2 per leg. This holds while m<sub>a</sub> ≤ 1, the linear range. Above 1 the reference passes the carrier peak, some carrier periods have no crossing, and low-order harmonics return; this is overmodulation, and as m<sub>a</sub> grows the output tends to the square wave, 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π for the full bridge.

Bipolar SPWM uses one reference for the whole bridge. When v<sub>r</sub> > carrier, S1 and S4 are on and v<sub>o</sub> = +V<sub>dc</sub>; otherwise S2 and S3 are on and v<sub>o</sub> = −V<sub>dc</sub>. The output has two levels and no zero state. Its fundamental peak is m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub>.

The harmonics sit at m<sub>f</sub> and its sidebands m<sub>f</sub> ± 2, m<sub>f</sub> ± 4, then around 2m<sub>f</sub> (2m<sub>f</sub> ± 1, 2m<sub>f</sub> ± 3), and so on. Choose m<sub>f</sub> odd, so that the wave has half-wave symmetry and no even harmonics. For m<sub>f</sub> of about 9 or more the harmonic amplitudes depend on m<sub>a</sub> but hardly on m<sub>f</sub>: at m<sub>a</sub> = 0.8 the m<sub>f</sub> harmonic is 0.818V<sub>dc</sub> peak and each m<sub>f</sub> ± 2 sideband 0.220V<sub>dc</sub>.

Unipolar SPWM switches the two legs separately: leg A compares +v<sub>r</sub> with the carrier and leg B compares −v<sub>r</sub> with the same carrier. When both top or both bottom switches are on, the load sees zero, so v<sub>o</sub> takes +V<sub>dc</sub>, 0 or −V<sub>dc</sub>. The fundamental is still m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub>, but the output pulses come twice per carrier period and the harmonics at m<sub>f</sub> and its sidebands cancel between the legs.

The first harmonic group is at 2m<sub>f</sub> ± 1: at m<sub>a</sub> = 0.8 each is 0.314V<sub>dc</sub> peak. The ripple is at twice the frequency and each step is only V<sub>dc</sub>, so the filter can be smaller, and the load sees half the voltage jumps. Each switch still switches at f<sub>c</sub>.

A three-phase bridge uses three references 120° apart and one carrier. Each pole voltage has a fundamental peak m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub>/2, so the line voltage fundamental is √3 times that. Choose m<sub>f</sub> odd and a multiple of 3: the carrier harmonic m<sub>f</sub> is then the same in all three poles and cancels in the line voltage, leaving m<sub>f</sub> ± 2 as the first group.
VL1 = 0.612 ma Vdc VL1 is the rms fundamental line voltage, (√3/2√2) ma Vdc, valid for ma ≤ 1.

Adding a third harmonic of one sixth of the fundamental to all three references flattens their tops, so m<sub>a</sub> can rise to 2/√3 = 1.155 before overmodulation. The added harmonic is the same in every phase, so it cancels in the line voltage. The usable line voltage rises by 15.5 %, to 0.707V<sub>dc</sub> rms, the same limit as space vector modulation.

figure.caption: The worked example’s modulator over one 20 ms cycle: a 0.8 sine against a 1050 Hz carrier. The bipolar output jumps between +400 V and −400 V; the unipolar output uses +400 V, 0 and −400 V, so its steps are half as large and its ripple sits near twice the carrier frequency.

spec.aria: Top: a sine reference of amplitude 0.8 and a triangular carrier with 21 cycles in one period. Middle: the bipolar output, a two-level pulse train. Bottom: the unipolar output, a three-level pulse train whose pulse widths follow the sine.

examples.question: A single-phase full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V and uses SPWM with f<sub>m</sub> = 50 Hz, m<sub>a</sub> = 0.8 and m<sub>f</sub> = 21. Find (a) the fundamental peak and rms, (b) the carrier frequency, (c) the frequencies and sizes of the first harmonic group for bipolar SPWM, and (d) the same for unipolar SPWM.
steps: (a) V<sub>1,peak</sub> = m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub> = 0.8 × 400 = 320 V; V<sub>1</sub> = 320/√2 = 226.3 V.
(c) Bipolar: the largest harmonic is at m<sub>f</sub>, 21 × 50 = 1050 Hz, of 0.818 × 400 = 327 V peak; the sidebands 19 and 23 (950 Hz and 1150 Hz) are each 0.220 × 400 = 88 V peak.
(d) Unipolar: the m<sub>f</sub> group cancels; the first group is 2m<sub>f</sub> ± 1 = 41 and 43, at 2050 Hz and 2150 Hz, each 0.314 × 400 = 126 V peak.
A filter that passes 50 Hz must attenuate 950 Hz for bipolar but only 2050 Hz for unipolar: more than twice as far from the fundamental.
examples.answer: 320 V peak (226.3 V rms); f<sub>c</sub> = 1050 Hz; bipolar: 327 V at 1050 Hz with 88 V sidebands at 950 and 1150 Hz; unipolar: 126 V at 2050 and 2150 Hz.

examples.question: A three-phase VSI has V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V, f<sub>m</sub> = 50 Hz, m<sub>f</sub> = 15 and m<sub>a</sub> = 0.9. Find the rms fundamental line voltage, the lowest harmonics in the line voltage, and the largest line voltage available with plain SPWM and with third-harmonic injection.
steps: m<sub>f</sub> = 15 is odd and a multiple of 3, so the 15th harmonic (750 Hz) cancels in the line voltage; the lowest are the 13th and 17th, at 650 Hz and 850 Hz.
Plain SPWM ends at m<sub>a</sub> = 1: V<sub>L1</sub> = 0.6124 × 600 = 367.4 V.
With third-harmonic injection m<sub>a</sub> can reach 1.155: V<sub>L1</sub> = 0.6124 × 1.155 × 600 = 424.3 V, which is 0.707V<sub>dc</sub>, 15.5 % more.
examples.answer: 330.7 V rms; first line-voltage harmonics at 650 Hz and 850 Hz; maximum 367.4 V with SPWM and 424.3 V with third-harmonic injection.

traps: Do not swap m<sub>a</sub> and m<sub>f</sub>: m<sub>a</sub> sets the voltage, m<sub>f</sub> sets where the harmonics are.
m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub> is a peak for the full bridge; divide by √2 for rms. For a three-phase pole it is m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub>/2.
Unipolar and bipolar SPWM give the same fundamental; unipolar moves the first harmonic group from m<sub>f</sub> to 2m<sub>f</sub> ± 1.
Above m<sub>a</sub> = 1 the fundamental is no longer m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub> and low-order harmonics appear.
Third-harmonic injection works because the third harmonic cancels between phases; it gives nothing to a single-phase load.

quiz.q: Define m<sub>a</sub> and m<sub>f</sub> for sine-triangle PWM.
quiz.a: m<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>r</sub>/V<sub>c</sub>, reference peak over carrier peak. m<sub>f</sub> = f<sub>c</sub>/f<sub>m</sub>, carrier frequency over reference frequency.

quiz.q: Why does SPWM move the unwanted harmonics to high frequency?
quiz.a: The duty ratio changes slowly at f<sub>m</sub>, so the average output is a sine at f<sub>m</sub>; the fast switching makes ripple only at the carrier frequency and its sidebands, far from the fundamental.

quiz.q: A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V, m<sub>a</sub> = 0.6, f<sub>m</sub> = 50 Hz and m<sub>f</sub> = 15. Find the fundamental rms and the carrier frequency.
quiz.a: V<sub>1,peak</sub> = 0.6 × 600 = 360 V, so V<sub>1</sub> = 254.6 V rms. f<sub>c</sub> = 15 × 50 = 750 Hz.

quiz.q: A three-phase VSI on a 540 V bus must give 300 V rms line to line with SPWM. Find m<sub>a</sub>.
Compare bipolar and unipolar SPWM for the same carrier frequency.
quiz.a: Both give m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub>. Bipolar has two levels, ±V<sub>dc</sub> jumps and its first harmonics at m<sub>f</sub>; unipolar has three levels, V<sub>dc</sub> jumps and its first harmonics at 2m<sub>f</sub> ± 1, so the filter is smaller and the ripple current lower. Unipolar needs the legs gated separately.

quiz.q: Why should m<sub>f</sub> be an odd multiple of 3 in a three-phase SPWM inverter?
quiz.a: Odd keeps half-wave symmetry, so no even harmonics. A multiple of 3 makes the m<sub>f</sub> harmonic identical in the three poles, so it cancels in the line voltage.
It lowers the reference peaks so m<sub>a</sub> can reach 1.155 without overmodulation, giving 15.5 % more line voltage; the third harmonic cancels between the lines.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital controllers make SPWM with timers and compare registers, updating the duty once per carrier period. Discontinuous PWM clamps one phase at a time to save switching loss, and random PWM spreads acoustic noise. Search for regular-sampled PWM and discontinuous PWM.
